A.explanation: Too small - at $6.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ the $6.0\text{ m}$ horizontal flight would take about $0.95\text{ s}$, in which time the vertical fall would be much more than $2.0\text{ m}$.

B.explanation: Correct - a $2.0\text{ m}$ vertical fall takes about $0.64\text{ s}$, so $v = 6.0/0.64$ gives about $9.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ horizontally.

C.explanation: Slightly too large - $9.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ would carry the cyclist further than $6.0\text{ m}$ in the time needed to fall $2.0\text{ m}$ vertically.

D.explanation: Much too large - $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ would cover $6.0\text{ m}$ in only $0.40\text{ s}$, allowing a vertical drop of only about $0.8\text{ m}$.

hints: Notice the launch is horizontal, so initial vertical velocity is zero while initial horizontal velocity is $v$ over the $6.0\text{ m}$ range.
Treat vertical fall of $2.0\text{ m}$ separately with $s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ to find the time of flight, since horizontal and vertical motions share the same time.
Divide the horizontal distance $6.0\text{ m}$ by that fall time to get $v$, because horizontal velocity stays constant with negligible air resistance.
walkthrough: Separate the motion: vertically the cyclist starts from rest and falls $s = 2.0\text{ m}$ with $a = g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$; horizontally velocity $v$ is constant.
Find time of flight from vertical motion using $s = u_yt + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $u_y = 0$, so $t = \sqrt{2s/g}$.
Use horizontal motion $x = vt$ with $x = 6.0\text{ m}$: $v = x/t = 6.0/0.64 \approx 9.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
